# From the Editor

In the turbulent wars of the twentieth century, nations' fates were often shaped by heroes. In the age of peace to come, it would be entrepreneurs who would steer the economy's tides.

The world is moving toward peace in the foreseeable future. Competition between nations is no longer measured in nuclear warheads but in economic strength. Three features define the economic contest of the twenty-first century: R&D as the backbone of national power; competitiveness as the barometer of rising and falling fortunes; and entrepreneurs as the central figures on the global stage.

From the vantage point of economic history, Joseph Schumpeter (1883–1950) was one of the first great economists of the early twentieth century to grasp the centrality of "innovation" and the "entrepreneur." He argued that clusters of innovation—automobiles, for instance—could utterly transform the way people live. It was the entrepreneur, the one who spotted opportunities and shouldered risk, who drove economic growth forward.

Schumpeter's insight is vividly confirmed by Taiwan's half-century of economic development. T.Y. Wang of Formosa Plastics embodied the meticulous management essential to an economy taking off; Morris Chang of TSMC embodied the vision required in the era of high technology.

Cheng & Man Publishing has undertaken, through its *Global Views* series, to publish works by those who played pivotal roles in Taiwan's development—broadly speaking, modern heroes and architects. Some carried the ambition of heroes; others the calling of nation-builders. In essays, biographies, and memoirs, these statesmen, entrepreneurs, and scholars have recounted their journeys with candor and systematic reflection, offering the eye of witnesses to history.

The publication of this autobiography by Morris Chang is especially noteworthy. At eighteen, he arrived from war-torn China at Harvard. For decades thereafter he studied and worked in the English-speaking world. That he now wrote his experiences—page by page—in his native tongue is itself a humanitarian achievement beyond the world of technology.

Among the many commentaries on Mr. Chang, two lines have stayed with me:

*Others praise his technological achievement, but Chang sees only responsibility. When the world admires his glory, Chang thinks only of service.*

Is it the relentless progress of Western science that keeps his gaze fixed on responsibility? Is it the quiet influence of Eastern culture that turns his thoughts toward service? Readers may find the answer within these pages.

This autobiography covers only half a life. We eagerly await the second half.

February 1998, Taipei

*The author is publisher of Cheng & Man Publishing Co., Ltd., Taiwan edition.*

---

## Author's Preface

### What an Otherworldly Time It Was!

**Morris Chang**
self_en:
The period covered in this autobiography runs from my birth to the age of thirty-three—exactly half the age I am now.

Busy men rarely have time to look back. Yet on quiet nights, when memory does come unbidden, I find I miss not the period after thirty-three, when my career had some modest success, but the first half of my life.

Before I turned eighteen, I had fled three times in evacuation, lived in six cities—Ningbo, Nanjing, Guangzhou, Hong Kong, Chongqing, and Shanghai—and attended ten different schools. I had known the sound of gunfire (in Hong Kong) and the thunder of bombing (in Guangzhou and Chongqing). I had crossed a war front, from Shanghai to Chongqing. I had enjoyed an untroubled childhood in Hong Kong, and later lived the impassioned, patriotic life of a high school student during the resistance war in Chongqing. And then came the sorrow of leaving home and country, never knowing when—or if—I would return, when I sailed from Hong Kong to America.

At eighteen, I entered Harvard University. Among more than a thousand classmates, I was the only Chinese. For a full year I had nothing but American friends and spoke nothing but English, and I absorbed Western culture the way a sponge absorbs water. Even now, decades later, that single year at Harvard remains the most unforgettable, the most electrifying of my life.

At nineteen I went to MIT, to the greatest engineering school in the world, to learn the skills that would put food on my table.

At twenty-four I entered the semiconductor industry, which itself was only three years old.

At twenty-seven I joined Texas Instruments, then at the height of its golden age. I drank coffee with Jack Kilby, the inventor of the integrated circuit, and talked research with him. I watched him invent it.

At thirty I picked up my satchel again and went to Stanford for a doctorate, to shore up my semiconductor scholarship before the great masters.

At thirty-three, doctorate in hand, I returned to TI, brimming with hope and expectation.

What an extraordinary era that was—extraordinary in China, extraordinary in America, extraordinary in the semiconductor industry. It was a "great age."

It was my youth.

It was the youth of the semiconductor industry.

It was also the youth of America in the heady years after it had become the world's preeminent power.

And even in ancient China, in those few years of the resistance war, one could sense a fierce, unmistakable breath of youth.

---

**The Distant and the Immediate Reasons for Writing This**

Beautiful nostalgia alone was not enough to set me to writing an autobiography. The decision to take up my pen had its distant causes and its immediate ones.

The distant cause goes back to a dream I harbored as a boy: to become a writer. For six or seven years, during my elementary days in Hong Kong and my middle school years in Chongqing and Shanghai, I naively imagined making writing my lifelong vocation. That dream was quietly extinguished by my father, who, upon my graduation from high school, simply remarked that it was a profession that would leave one starving. I came to America, and in the thirty-odd years that followed, I wrote almost nothing in Chinese—hardly even reading Chinese books or newspapers. It was only when I came to Taiwan more than a decade ago, beginning to write in Chinese again, that the boyhood dream surfaced as memory. Sometimes I asked myself: Can I still write a substantial work in Chinese?

That question remained unanswered for more than twenty years.

Then, just over two years ago, a friend, Yu You-cheng, asked me to write a foreword for his new book, *My View of Intel*. He said two thousand words would suffice. But after reading his manuscript, I found myself deeply moved by the passage he had written about Intel's history. I spent an entire Sunday writing freely, and ended up with four or five thousand words. It was one of the few lengthy Chinese pieces I had written in decades, and to my surprise, it came fairly easily.

A few months later, Professor Gao Xijun, the publisher of Mr. Yu's book, came to see me. He suggested that among the experiences of my life there must be many interesting stories worth sharing with readers in the form of an autobiography. He also offered an alternative: if I did not wish to write it myself, I could dictate, and a professional journalist would put it on paper.

I have never cared for the dictated biography. Having read many of them, I always felt they lacked something essential—the personal feeling of the subject. But to write it myself? What a daunting and time-consuming undertaking. Did I have the ability? The time? For several weeks I gave Professor Gao no answer.

---

**To Remember Is Pleasure; To Write Is Torment**

It was then, one evening, that I happened to reread a collection of Hemingway's short stories—the one I loved best—and came to "The Snows of Kilimanjaro." The protagonist is a writer who, struck by gangrene at the foot of Kilimanjaro in Africa, lies waiting to die while gazing at the snow-covered peak. Here are his last, drifting thoughts:

Now he would never write those stories anymore, the ones he had stored up, hoping to write them someday when he was a better writer. Perhaps at least he had not spoiled them. Perhaps he would never be a better writer, and that was the very reason he had kept putting them off. Anyway, it was all unknown now.

The consequence of procrastination, I realized, is nothing less than the helplessness and uncertainty of life's final pages. A few days after reading that passage, I accepted Professor Gao's invitation. I would write my own autobiography.

But every time I sat down to write, I regretted it. I had agreed too hastily! For me, reminiscence is a pleasure; putting it on paper is torment. Many nights and weekends I sat at my desk, pen in hand, staring blankly at a sheet of white paper. Emotions surged within me, yet were trapped inside the narrow barrel of that short fountain pen, unable to flow freely onto the page. Including the time spent gathering materials, this autobiography consumed several hundred hours.

The passage of fifty or sixty years, so many evacuations, so many move—by the time I reached eighteen, very little material remained. This is a profound loss, precisely because that was the period when I most wanted to be a writer, and I kept journals and wrote regularly. But my diaries before the age of sixteen are gone entirely. Only a handful of essays survived, and those only because Nankai High School in Chongqing kept them for decades, publishing a few of them several years ago in an alumni memoir. Reading them now, though the writing is plainly immature, brought back a wealth of memories. Among the lost pieces, the most regrettable was a travelogue I wrote after my fifty-something-day trek from Shanghai to Chongqing—I remember my parents proudly showing it to their friends.

Miraculously, diaries from my time in Shanghai at sixteen or seventeen resurfaced more than twenty years ago in my parents' home in New York. Those accounts of the period just before and after my high school graduation, as the Communist forces closed in on Shanghai, read now like the record of another lifetime. Materials from after I turned eighteen are somewhat more plentiful, though far from abundant. The most useful remain the sporadic, intermittently kept diaries.

---

**The Second Volume: Perhaps in a Few Years**

Before the first volume was even published, people were already asking about the second. To be honest, having expended so much energy and time on this volume, and with my current responsibilities laying the groundwork for TSMC and World Advanced, I have not the courage to begin the second one in the near term. Perhaps in a few years.

At last, the first volume is done. It has been an emotional journey—two years of concentrated labor, hundreds of hours, filled with warmth and with torment. And now, at last, I can exhale.

Today, my mood is not unlike what I felt on a day more than thirty years ago. I had passed my doctoral examination at Stanford University. I let out a great sigh of relief, drove thirty miles that evening to San Francisco's Chinatown, and ate a hearty meal. Afterward I went to a bridge club and played cards for the first time in six months (see Chapter 5).

Will today be the same? More than thirty years have swept past me. I may carry the same feelings as back then, but I no longer have the same zest.
